problems.title: Pauli sampling reseeded on every call
claim: Repeated Pauli-channel calls sample the specified stochastic channel.
analysis: The current official supplemental LindbladError.apply and InverseLindbladError.apply each call random.seed(54) internally before drawing Pauli events. Fixed parameters therefore repeat the same Pauli event pattern on every call; quantum measurement randomness does not restore independent Pauli-channel sampling. With one \(Z\) Pauli and \(\lambda=\sigma=0.1\), the event probability is \((1-e^{-0.2})/2\approx0.0906346\), while the repeated first uniform value is \(0.913643\), selecting identity each time. For input \(|0\rangle\) and observable \(Z\), the true inverse-channel expectation is \(1\), but the released identity/sign selection multiplied by \(\Gamma=e^{0.2}\) yields \(1.221402758\). This exact bias does not decrease with more calls. Historical classification-run impact is unknown; no author program was executed in this recheck.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Initialize a persistent RNG once per run and redraw each shot; verify transition matrices and rerun experiments.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: L2 concentration guarantee omits dimension
problems.source_location: PDF pp.38–40, Lemma A.22, Theorem A.23, equations 31–33
claim: The coordinatewise concentration argument supplies the stated vector-L \(2\) guarantee.
analysis: The proof reverses event inclusion: \(\|e\|_\infty\ge\epsilon\) implies \(\|e\|_2\ge\epsilon\), but not conversely. For instance \((0.8,0.8)\) has both coordinates below one and Euclidean norm above one.

A legal one-qubit instance uses \(\rho=I/2\), \(M=Z\), label \(y=1\), and \(1000\) fixed unitary layers, each with one inverse-noise coordinate, all true and inverse noise parameters zero at the evaluated point. Every true gradient is zero because the maximally mixed state is invariant. Select every coordinate, \(p=\Gamma=\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=0.05\), and \(N=5426\) shots per coordinate, split into independent batches of \(n=2713\). Algorithm 3 gives \(g_j=-4(1-A_j)B_j\), with independent Rademacher sample means \(A_j,B_j\); Algorithm 5 independently calls these coordinate estimates. This is the paper’s ideal independent-sampling algorithm, separate from the released reseeding defect.

Put \(\mu_2=1/n\), \(\mu_4=3/n^2-2/n^3\). Then \(\mathbb Eg_j^2=16(1+\mu_2)\mu_2\) and \(\mathbb Eg_j^4=256(1+6\mu_2+\mu_4)\mu_4\). For \(Z=\sum_{j=1}^{1000}g_j^2\), these give \(\mathbb EZ\simeq5.8997042\) and \(\mathbb EZ^2\simeq34.8762510\). Paley-Zygmund yields \(\Pr(Z>1)\ge(\mathbb EZ-1)^2/\mathbb EZ^2\simeq0.688351\), whereas the printed tail bound is \(2d\exp(-2N/32^2)\simeq0.049949\).

The printed Theorem A.23 says “at least,” which is a necessary-budget claim. The witness directly refutes Lemma A.22 and Eqs. (31)–(32), and shows that solving that tail bound does not provide a sufficient Euclidean-error budget. It does not by itself refute the same smaller number as a possible necessary lower bound; a sufficient concentration argument also cannot establish information-theoretic necessity.
result: Lemma A.22's Euclidean tail guarantee is false, and the derived sufficient shot budget is not established. Theorem A.23's literal necessary-budget wording is not separately refuted by this counterexample; sufficiency does not establish necessity.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Applying the coordinate tail bound at \(\epsilon/\sqrt m\) gives the sufficient budget \(N\ge512\Gamma^4m\epsilon^{-2}\log(2m/\delta)\) per selected coordinate, rounded to an allowed even value. This is not an optimality lower bound. Alternatively restrict the guarantee to the infinity norm.
problems.impact_rationale: An exact moment/probability calculation violates the core Euclidean gradient-estimation guarantee by a wide margin, exposing the missing dimension dependence.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Pauli parameter-shift convention mismatch
problems.source_location: PDF p.2 Eq 1, p.5 Eq 8, pp.26–27, p.31 Algorithm 4; Implementation/Experiments.py:183–200
claim: The parameter-shift coefficient matches the declared Pauli-gate convention.
analysis: For \(U(\theta)=e^{i\theta X}\), choose an expectation \(f(\theta)=\cos2\theta\). The printed half-difference with shifts \(\pm\pi/2\) is zero, but \(f'(\theta)=-2\sin2\theta\), approximately \(-1.3485758\) at \(\theta=0.37\). These gate/shift conventions cannot be combined.

The current HEA source instead uses Qiskit half-angle RX/RY/RZ gates, shifts \(\pm\pi/4\) and coefficient \(1/\sqrt2\), which form a valid generalized shift for that half-angle convention. The printed zero-derivative witness is therefore not attributed to that HEA branch. The generic exponential gate Tools.unitary_exponent explicitly implements \(\cos\theta I+i\sin\theta P\); its use of the same coefficient rescales the correct derivative by \(1/\sqrt2\). A later sign update can hide a positive scale difference, but is not the claimed unbiased gradient implementation.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: For \(e^{i\theta P}\), use the full difference at \(\theta\pm\pi/4\), or define half-angle gates and use the corresponding standard half-difference at \(\pm\pi/2\).
problems.impact_rationale: The gate definition and parameter-shift identity give different derivatives on a single-qubit observable. This invalidates a central analytic gradient formula.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Summable steps do not guarantee stationarity
claim: Summable steps imply the claimed stationary convergence.
analysis: For the allowed quantum loss \(F(\theta,\sigma)=(1-e^{2\sigma}\cos2\theta)^2\), use \(\theta\in[0,\pi/2]\), \(\sigma\in[0,1/1024]\), initial \((\pi/8,0)\), and \(\eta_t=2^{-t-12}\). The total step is \(1/2048\).

Every sampled \(\theta\)-gradient estimate has magnitude at most \(4\Gamma_{\max}(1+\Gamma_{\max})\simeq8.0234757\), with \(\Gamma_{\max}=e^{2/1024}\). Nonexpansive projection therefore keeps every path in \[[0.388781369,0.396616794]\]. Throughout this interval and the full \(\sigma\) box, \(\partial_\theta F\ge4(1-\Gamma_{\max}\cos2\ell)\sin2\ell\simeq0.80251458>0\), where \(\ell=\pi/8-4\Gamma_{\max}(1+\Gamma_{\max})/2048\). Thus no path approaches a constrained stationary point.

The current Theorem A.31 actually states a finite weighted objective-gap upper bound with a nonvanishing constant. The all-path witness refutes the further stationarity interpretation under its permitted summable steps, rather than supplying a numerical violation of that nonzero upper bound. The proof of that upper bound separately contains the smoothness and second-moment errors below.
result: The summable-step conditions do not justify the stationary-convergence interpretation. This does not numerically refute the theorem's distinct finite-time objective-gap bound, which contains a nonvanishing constant.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Use projected-gradient residual, smoothness and a valid stochastic projected method; require conditions that permit sufficient total movement and control sampling error.
problems.impact_rationale: An admissible positive-width quantum parameter box and all-path displacement bound contradict the claimed stationary-convergence interpretation.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Function-Lipschitz constant substituted for gradient smoothness
claim: The function-Lipschitz constant is sufficient for the descent lemma used.
analysis: For \(F(x)=x^2\) on \([0,0.1]\), the function-Lipschitz constant is \(0.2\), but gradient smoothness requires constant \(2\). Substitution into the claimed quadratic upper model at \(x=0\), \(y=0.1\), would require \(0.01\le0.001\), which is false. The convergence proof must distinguish those two constants.

The lemma explicitly concerns general continuously differentiable functions; the displayed example refutes that lemma. The paper’s particular analytic quantum loss can have a finite Hessian bound on a compact box, but that requires a distinct smoothness constant and does not validate the printed substitution.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Use a gradient-smoothness constant \(H=\sup_{x\in C}\|\nabla^2F(x)\|_2\) on the compact parameter set, distinct from function Lipschitzness.
problems.impact_rationale: The convergence proof substitutes function Lipschitzness for gradient smoothness; the resulting descent inequality is false even for a scalar quadratic.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Second moment bounded by central variance
problems.source_location: PDF p.44 after Eq 37; PropositionA 30 pp.42–43
claim: Central variance directly upper-bounds the gradient second moment.
analysis: The correct identity is \(\mathbb E\|g\|^2=\operatorname{Var}(g)+\|\mathbb Eg\|^2\). A deterministic gradient \(g=1\) has variance zero and second moment one. A central-variance bound cannot replace a second-moment bound without the squared-mean term.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Use a uniform second-moment bound or add squared mean and all conditional-variance components.
problems.impact_rationale: A deterministic nonzero gradient refutes the second-moment substitution used in the convergence argument. The omitted squared mean is a substantial derivation error.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Experiments implement sequential sign-Adam rather than stated proximal SGD
claim: The experiments implement the stated synchronous proximal-gradient algorithm.
analysis: The current supplemental description acknowledges Adam, whereas the paper states proximal SGD. ExperimentsHEA.py turns the theta estimate into its sign and immediately updates that coordinate; the sigma path also returns a sign. GenericNoiseMitigatedUnitaryCircuit.py applies Adam and clips the parameters. Later coordinate estimates therefore see changed parameters, while their residual can still come from the start-of-round prediction. This differs from synchronous gradient collection at one parameter point and from coordinate descent with a freshly evaluated residual. These variants may work empirically, but their reported results are not direct verification of the stated synchronous projected-SGD theorem.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Freeze parameter snapshot, gather gradients then update synchronously, or clearly specify and analyze the actual variant.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Precision and coordinate-sampling explanations inaccurate
claim: The precision and coordinate-sampling explanations have the stated algebraic meaning.
analysis: The \(\epsilon^{-2}\) dependence is polynomial in inverse precision, while the \(\Gamma\) factor can carry exponential dependence. Also \(d/p>0\) for finite positive \(p\); a claimed zero expected coordinate count is not obtained by merely increasing \(p\). Absolute vector precision alone does not guarantee signs of components whose true magnitudes are smaller than the noise scale.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Describe quadratic inverse-precision and exponential mitigation-factor dependence separately. Interpret \(p\le d\) as expected selected count at least one, and use componentwise signal/noise conditions for sign claims.
